questions.q:
A tourist in Jaipur carries two maps. The old-city guide map uses the scale 1 cm = 400 m. Her atlas map of India shows a scale ruler 2.5 cm long marked 500 km.
(a) How much ground does 1 cm stand for on the atlas map?
(b) How many times as much ground is that as 1 cm on the guide map?
(c) On the guide map the palace and the fort are 3 cm apart. Find the ground distance, and then how long that same distance would be drawn on the atlas map.
(d) Using (c), explain why the atlas map cannot show the palace and the fort as two separate places.
(e) She says, 'The atlas map is the more accurate one, because it shows the whole country.' Judge her statement.
questions.a: (a) 500 km / 2.5 = 200 km per cm. (b) 200 km = 2,00,000 m, and 2,00,000 / 400 = 500 times. (c) 3 x 400 m = 1,200 m = 1.2 km; on the atlas map 1.2 / 200 = 0.006 cm, which is 0.06 mm. (d) 0.06 mm is far too small to draw or see, so both places fall on the same point; the atlas can only mark Jaipur as one place. (e) She is wrong: neither map is more accurate in general. Each map uses its own scale; the atlas suits a whole-country area, but for a walk between the palace and the fort only the guide map's scale gives a usable distance.
s: Part (a): 1 cm = 200 km on the atlas map
Part (b): 500 times the guide map figure
Part (c): 1.2 km on the ground, only 0.006 cm on the atlas map
Part (d): the two places would fall on one point, so Jaipur appears as one place
Part (e): rejects the claim; each scale suits its own area and purpose

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A map of a village in Tamil Nadu drawn with the Survey of India's symbols can be read in the same way by an office in Assam.
Reason (R): Different countries use different sets of map symbols.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but R does not explain A. A is true because the Survey of India has fixed one set of symbols for maps of India, so offices across India read them the same way. R is also true, but it is about differences between countries, which does not explain why two Indian offices agree.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Two maps show the same two towns. On map P the towns are 4 cm apart; on map Q they are 8 cm apart. Ravi says the towns must be farther apart on map Q's ground. Which reply is correct?
questions.a: Same ground distance; each cm on map Q stands for half the ground of map P. The distance between two real towns does not change; actual distance depends on the scale the map uses.
o: Same ground distance; 1 cm on map Q shows half the ground of map P
Ravi is right, because a longer line on a map always means a longer road
Map P is the correct one, because a smaller drawing is always more exact
Neither map can be used, because maps do not show distance on the ground

questions.q:
Class 6 must draw their school compound, which is 360 m long, on a chart where only 20 cm of length can be used.
(a) Which of these scales will fit the compound on the chart: 1 cm = 10 m, 1 cm = 20 m, 1 cm = 50 m? Show the working.
(b) Using (a), which fitting scale gives the biggest drawing, and how long will the compound be drawn?
questions.a: (a) 360 / 10 = 36 cm (does not fit); 360 / 20 = 18 cm (fits); 360 / 50 = 7.2 cm (fits). So 1 cm = 20 m and 1 cm = 50 m fit. (b) 1 cm = 20 m, because each centimetre stands for less ground; the compound is drawn 18 cm long.
s: Part (a): 36, 18 and 7.2 cm worked out; the 20 m and 50 m scales fit
Part (b): 1 cm = 20 m, drawn 18 cm long

questions.q: Write a situation, with a place, a map scale and a measured map distance, whose answer is 'The two places are 4.5 km apart on the ground.' Then show the working.
questions.a: Any consistent situation, for example: On a map of Mysuru with the scale 1 cm = 250 m, the palace and the bus stand are 18 cm apart. Working: 18 x 250 m = 4,500 m = 4.5 km.
s: A situation naming a place and giving a scale
A map measurement that matches the scale
Working that reaches 4.5 km

questions.q:
A wall map of Kerala shows the Western Ghats shaded brown and the rivers in blue, and also marks the district boundaries with each district's headquarters.
(a) Which features on it are those of a physical map, and which are those of a political map?
(b) Reena only needs to find which districts the Periyar river flows through. Explain why this map serves her better than a map with only one of the two kinds of feature.
questions.a: (a) Physical: the Ghats (mountains) and the rivers, which are natural features. Political: the district boundaries and headquarters. (b) Her question joins a natural feature (the river) to political units (districts). A physical-only map would not show the districts, and a political-only map might not show the river, so she needs both on one sheet.
s: Part (a): Ghats and rivers are physical; boundaries and headquarters are political
Part (b): her question needs both the river and the districts

questions.q: Arjun says: 'A map is just a smaller copy of a place, so every map, whether of a village or of all of India, shows each building in it.' Is he right? Give reasons.
questions.a: Partly right. He is right that a map represents an area, small or very large, viewed from the top and fitted onto paper using a scale. He is wrong that every map shows each building: on the map of a large city or a country there is not enough space to draw them all, so symbols stand for kinds of buildings and many details are left out.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: a map represents an area of any size from above, fitted using a scale
Wrong part: large-area maps lack space, so symbols replace drawings of buildings

questions.q:
On a trekking map the arrow marked N points to the right-hand edge of the page, not to the top.
(a) The well is drawn directly above the school. In which direction is the well from the school?
(b) The pond is drawn below and to the right of the school. In which direction is the pond from the school?
questions.a: (a) Going clockwise from north (right edge): east is at the bottom, south at the left, west at the top. So 'above' is west: the well is west of the school. (b) Below is east and right is north, so the pond is northeast of the school.
s: Part (a): west, after turning the directions clockwise from the arrow
Part (b): northeast (below = east, right = north)

questions.q:
Read the statements about maps.
1. A drawing of one village and a drawing of the whole world, both viewed from the top, can each be called a map.
2. An atlas is a single large map of the whole world printed on one sheet.
3. When a map must show one specific kind of information, a thematic map is the right kind.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are correct: a map may show a small area or a very large one, and a thematic map carries a specific kind of information. 2 is false: an atlas is a book or collection of maps.

questions.q:
Nandini has just moved to Pune. Her map has the scale 1 cm = 200 m and an arrow marked N pointing to the top. The post office is drawn 3.5 cm from the railway station, up and to the right.
(a) How far is the post office from the station on the ground?
(b) In which direction must she head from the station?
(c) Using (b), in which direction must she head to come back?
(d) How far will she walk there and back?
(e) If the arrow had been torn off the map, which of your answers (a)-(d) could she still trust, and which not? Explain.
questions.a: (a) 3.5 x 200 m = 700 m. (b) Up is north and right is east, so northeast. (c) The opposite direction, southwest. (d) 2 x 700 m = 1,400 m = 1.4 km. (e) She could still trust (a) and (d), because distance comes from the scale. She could not trust (b) and (c): without the arrow she cannot tell which way north is, so 'up and to the right' no longer gives a direction.
s: Part (a): 700 m
Part (b): northeast
Part (c): southwest, the opposite of (b)
Part (d): 1.4 km
Part (e): distances still hold; directions fail without the arrow

questions.q:
A town map has north at the top and the scale 1 cm = 300 m. The bank is drawn 2 cm to the right of the railway station. The market is drawn 3 cm directly above the bank, and the lake is drawn 3 cm directly above the station.
(a) In which direction is the market from the station?
(b) In which direction is the lake from the bank?
(c) In which cardinal direction is the lake from the market, and how far apart are they on the ground?
questions.a: (a) The market is up and to the right of the station: northeast. (b) The lake is up and to the left of the bank: northwest. (c) The lake and the market are both 3 cm above the line through the station and the bank, so the lake is due west of the market, 2 cm away: 2 x 300 m = 600 m.
s: Part (a): northeast
Part (b): northwest
Part (c): west, 600 m

questions.q: The scale ruler on an atlas map of India is 2.5 cm long and marked 500 km. Two cities are 6 cm apart on this map. How far apart are they on the ground?
questions.a: 1,200 km: 500 / 2.5 = 200 km per cm, and 6 x 200 = 1,200 km. 3,000 km reads the whole ruler as 1 cm; 7,500 km multiplies by 2.5 instead of dividing; 120 km drops a zero.

questions.q: A map uses the scale 1 cm = 250 m. A straight road 2 km long will be drawn ___ cm long on it.

Three maps are printed on sheets of the same size: a map of Kerala, a map of one village in Wayanad, and a map of India.
(a) Arrange them from the smallest area shown to the largest.
(b) Using (a), on which map does 1 cm stand for the greatest distance on the ground? Explain.
questions.a: (a) The village in Wayanad, then Kerala, then India. (b) The map of India: the largest area has to fit on the same size of sheet, so each centimetre must stand for the most ground.
s: Part (a): village, Kerala, India
Part (b): India, because the largest area on the same sheet needs the most ground per cm

questions.q: Meera prints a map of India that shows nothing but the areas where rice is grown, with State borders drawn faintly only to help readers. Her friend calls it a political map because the borders are visible. Which label fits Meera's map best?
questions.a: A thematic map: its purpose is one specific kind of information (where rice is grown). Faint borders do not make it a political map; it is not mainly about natural features (physical), and one map is not an atlas.

questions.q: For a project titled 'Map of my school', Kabir draws the front of his school building as seen from the gate, showing its windows, doors and roof. His teacher says it is a good picture but not a map. Why?
questions.a: A map looks at the surface as if viewing it from the top. Kabir drew the building from the front. A map does not need to be of a big area, need not be printed, and can show buildings, so those reasons are wrong.
o: A map shows the surface as if viewed from the top
A map must always show an area as big as a district
A map can only be printed by the Survey of India
A map may show roads and rivers but never buildings

questions.q: Shreya sends a friend a sketch to reach her house. It shows the roads and a small drawing of the temple near her lane, but it has no north arrow and no scale. (a) Name the two components of a map missing from the sketch. (b) Give one problem each missing component will cause her friend.
questions.a: (a) Direction and distance (scale). (b) Without the north arrow the friend cannot tell which way is north, east, south or west on the sketch; without a scale she cannot work out how far the house actually is.
s: Part (a): direction and distance (scale) are missing
Part (b): one problem each, cannot tell which way to go, cannot tell how far

questions.q:
A gram panchayat in Odisha will send the district office a hand-drawn map of its village. The office must plan a new road running straight from the school to the highway and order material for the road's full length. Both copies of the map show the school and the highway. Copy P has the scale 1 cm = 100 m but no north arrow, and shows the temple, the well and a small canal as little home-made pictures. Copy Q has a north arrow and Survey of India symbols, which any government office reads the same way, but no scale.
(a) If the whole district were drawn on one sheet, why would the little pictures have to become symbols?
(b) On Copy P the school is 7.5 cm from the highway. How long must the road be?
(c) What would the office be unable to do if it received only Copy Q?
(d) The panchayat can send only one copy. Which should it send? Justify by weighing what each copy gives the office and what each one lacks.
questions.a: (a) A map of a large area has no space to draw every building; symbols let many details fit in limited space. (b) 7.5 x 100 m = 750 m. (c) It could not turn any map length into a ground distance, so it could not work out how much material to order. (d) Copy P. Copy Q has real advantages: its north arrow gives directions, and its standard symbols can be read without guessing what a home-made picture means, while Copy P lacks both. But the road is fixed by its two ends, the school and the highway, which both copies show, so the office does not need compass directions to plan it; and the canal and well can be read from P's pictures with some care. The length for the material order can come only from a scale, and only Copy P has one, so P is the copy the task cannot do without.
s: Part (a): pictures become symbols for lack of space on a large-area map
Part (b): 750 m
Part (c): no scale, so no ground distance and no material estimate
Part (d): Copy P; Q's arrow and standard symbols help, but the road is fixed by its two ends and only P's scale gives the length

questions.q:
Match each need in Column A with the item that best serves it in Column B.
Column A: 1. A trekker wants to see where the mountains and rivers of a State lie  2. A quiz asks for the capital city of each State  3. A report must show only the rainfall of each district  4. A student wants maps of many countries in one book
Column B: a. thematic map  b. atlas  c. physical map  d. political map
questions.a: Mountains and rivers are natural features (physical map); States and capitals are political details; rainfall alone is one specific kind of information (thematic map); many maps in one book is an atlas.

questions.q: On a city map whose north arrow points to the top of the page, the school is drawn directly to the right of the railway station, and the hospital is drawn directly below the school. In which direction is the hospital from the station?
questions.a: Right of the page is east and below is south, so the hospital lies south and east of the station: southeast. Northeast mixes up up and down; southwest mixes up left and right; east ignores the move south.

questions.q:
A Class 6 teacher in Bhopal plans a walking trip. On a map with the scale 1 cm = 250 m she measures from the school:
| Place | Map distance | Direction |
| Museum | 6 cm | northeast |
| Public garden | 3.2 cm | west |
| Lake | 8.4 cm | south |
The class walks to one place and back the same way, at about 50 m per minute, and has 75 minutes of walking time.
(a) How far is the museum from the school on the ground?
(b) How long would the round trip to the public garden take?
(c) How long is the round trip to the lake, in km?
(d) The children want the lake because it is the farthest. The teacher wants the longest walk that still fits inside the 75 minutes. Which place meets the teacher's condition? Justify with the time each round trip takes.
questions.a: (a) 6 x 250 m = 1,500 m = 1.5 km. (b) 3.2 x 250 = 800 m each way, 1,600 m in all; 1,600 / 50 = 32 minutes. (c) 8.4 x 250 = 2,100 m each way, so 4.2 km there and back. (d) The museum. The lake round trip takes 4,200 / 50 = 84 minutes, more than the 75 available, so it fails. The museum (3,000 m, 60 minutes) and the garden (32 minutes) both fit, and the museum is the longer of the two walks, so it is the longest walk that fits.
s: Part (a): 1.5 km
Part (b): 32 minutes
Part (c): 4.2 km
Part (d): the museum; lake 84 minutes is over 75, and of the two that fit the museum (60 min) is longer than the garden (32 min)

questions.q: True or False? 'A map can show directions only if all four arrows, N, E, S and W, are drawn on it.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Most maps simply have one arrow marked 'N' pointing north. Once north is known, east, south and west follow clockwise from it, so one arrow is enough.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: one arrow marked N is enough, since E, S and W follow clockwise from north

questions.q: An online shop advertises a 'World Mat': a flat, printed mat of the whole Earth 'made by pressing a globe's map flat, with every country shown at its true shape and size, and no gaps or stretched parts'. Show that this claim cannot be true.
questions.a: The globe's map covers a sphere, the same shape as the Earth. The skin of a sphere cannot be pressed flat without tearing or stretching at the edges, as large pieces of orange peel tear when flattened. So a flat mat must have gaps or stretched parts somewhere, and cannot show every country at its true shape and size: a sphere cannot be represented accurately on a flat sheet.
s: The globe's map lies on a sphere
A curved surface tears or stretches when pressed flat (orange-peel idea)
So no flat mat can show every country at true shape and size

questions.q: A craft club is turning a plain plastic ball into a globe. Where should they draw the Equator?
questions.a: Halfway between the two poles, which are the points that stay fixed when the ball spins. A circle through both poles is a meridian; the top point is a pole; any circle would not be halfway.
o: Halfway between the two points that stay still when it spins
Round the ball through the two points that stay still
At the topmost point of the ball as it sits on its stand
Round the ball anywhere at all, so long as the circle is neat

questions.q:
Your class has a plain cardboard ball on a rod that lets it spin, and wants to turn it into a globe of the Earth.
(a) How will you find the two poles on it?
(b) Using (a), where will you draw the Equator?
(c) A classmate says the Equator alone is enough to show where Bhopal is. Using (b), explain why it is not.
(d) Which lines will you add to solve the problem in (c), and how do the two kinds of line differ in shape?
(e) Another classmate wants to mark Bhopal using only the meridian through it, with no parallels. Using (c) and (d), explain why that fails as well.
questions.a: (a) Spin the ball: the two points at the top and bottom that stay fixed are the poles. (b) The Equator is the circle halfway between the two poles. (c) The Equator is a whole circle round the ball; it only tells you whether a place is north or south of it, so Bhopal could be anywhere in the north. (d) Parallels of latitude, east-west circles that grow smaller towards the poles, and meridians of longitude, half-circles from pole to pole; together they form a grid that gives every place two coordinates. (e) A meridian is a half-circle running from pole to pole, so knowing only Bhopal's meridian leaves it anywhere along that line, from the North Pole to the South Pole; just as one parallel was not enough in (c), one meridian is not enough. Only where Bhopal's parallel and its meridian cross is the point fixed.
s: Part (a): the fixed points of the spin are the poles
Part (b): the Equator halfway between the poles
Part (c): one circle cannot fix a point; Bhopal could be anywhere north of it
Part (d): parallels (shrinking circles) and meridians (pole-to-pole half-circles) as a grid
Part (e): one meridian runs pole to pole, so Bhopal could be anywhere on it; only the crossing of both lines fixes it

questions.q: A science centre in Bengaluru sells a sphere with the craters and plains of the Moon drawn on it. Aman says it cannot be called a globe. Which statement settles the matter?
questions.a: A globe is a sphere on which a map is drawn, and the map may be of the Earth, the Moon, Mars or the sky. So the Moon sphere is a globe. Material and the number of maps do not decide it.
o: It is a globe: any sphere with a map drawn on it is one
Aman is right, because a globe must always show the Earth
Aman is right, because a globe has to be made of metal
It is an atlas, because it shows a map of a whole body

questions.q:
A desk lamp shines on one side of a globe in a dark room, and the globe is turned slowly eastward, from west to east, as the Earth spins.
(a) A town on the globe is just moving out of the shadow into the light. Is it morning or evening there? Explain.
(b) Kolkata is at about 88°E and Mumbai at about 73°E. Which of the two moves into the light first as the globe turns? Explain using (a).
questions.a: (a) Morning: the town is turning towards the lamp, which stands for the Sun, so its day is beginning; a town moving from light into shadow would be at evening. (b) Kolkata. The globe turns from west to east, so the more easterly place (88°E against 73°E, 15 degrees farther east) turns out of the shadow first and its morning comes earlier than Mumbai's.
s: Part (a): morning, the town is turning into the lamp's light
Part (b): Kolkata, the more easterly city turns into the light first

questions.q: Which of these tasks is better done with a flat map than with a globe of the Earth?
questions.a: Finding a route between two places in a small town needs a map of that small area with its streets. The other three tasks are about the whole Earth's round shape, which the globe shows better.
o: Finding a route from the station to a bank in a town
Seeing the true shape of the whole Earth all at once
Showing a whole class that the Earth is round in shape
Finding the North and South Poles by spinning it

questions.q:
A cheap globe has only one line drawn on it, the Equator. A radio message says a fishing boat is 'exactly on the Equator'.
(a) Why can Meena still not mark the boat's position on this globe?
(b) Which kind of line must be added to the globe, and how would it fix the problem?
questions.a: (a) The Equator is a full circle around the Earth, so the boat could be anywhere along it; the message gives only one coordinate. (b) Meridians of longitude, half-circles running from pole to pole. Each crosses the Equator at one point, so knowing the boat's meridian as well fixes one point; together the lines form a grid.
s: Part (a): the Equator is a whole circle, so one coordinate is not enough
Part (b): meridians, which cross the Equator at single points and complete the grid

questions.q:
A shop in Lucknow lists four items.
| Item | Shape and material | What is drawn on it |
| P | sphere, plastic | map of the Earth |
| Q | sphere, cardboard | the stars and constellations of the sky |
| R | flat sheet | map of the whole world |
| S | flat sheet | map of Lucknow city |
(a) Which items are globes? Why does Q count even though it shows no country?
(b) A visitor wants to find a hotel near Lucknow's railway station. Which item should she use, and why not P?
(c) A teacher wants one item that shows Class 6 the Earth's round shape and lets them find its poles. Which item should she choose, and how will the class find the poles with it?
questions.a: (a) P and Q. A globe is a sphere on which a map is drawn; that map may be of the stars and constellations, so Q is a globe. (b) S, the city map: it shows a small area, the streets near the station; P shows the whole Earth. (c) P: it is a sphere with the Earth's map, the same shape as the Earth. Spin it: the two fixed points at the top and bottom are the poles. Q shows the sky, not the Earth, and R is flat.
s: Part (a): P and Q; any sphere with a map is a globe
Part (b): S, a map of a small area with its streets
Part (c): P, a sphere with the Earth's map; the poles are the fixed points when it spins

questions.q:
Meena places a desk lamp on one side of a globe in a dark room and turns the globe slowly. She watches Delhi (77°E) and New York (74°W).
(a) What does the lamp stand for, and in which direction must she turn the globe to copy the real Earth?
(b) When Delhi faces the lamp directly, is New York more likely to be in light or in shadow? Use the gap in longitude between the two cities to explain.
(c) As she keeps turning in the direction from (a), does Delhi move next towards evening or towards morning?
(d) Using (b), explain why breakfast time in one country can be the middle of the night in another.
(e) Why does this model mean that measuring a place's longitude also tells us something about its time?
questions.a: (a) The Sun lighting the Earth; she turns the globe eastward (from west to east), as the Earth spins. (b) Shadow: the cities are 74 + 77 = 151 degrees apart, which is more than a quarter of the way round (90 of 360 degrees); a point more than 90 degrees round from the place facing the lamp directly is on the side turned away from it, so New York is in shadow. (c) Towards evening: Delhi has passed mid-day and moves on towards the edge of the light. (d) At one and the same moment, places at different positions round the globe face the lamp differently: one is moving into the light (morning) while one on the far side is in shadow (night). (e) A place's longitude fixes how far round the globe it is from another place, and that decides when it faces the Sun; so the longitude of a place also marks its time.
s: Part (a): the Sun; turn eastward
Part (b): shadow; 151 degrees apart, more than 90 degrees from the lit point
Part (c): towards evening
Part (d): at one moment, different positions mean different times of day
Part (e): position round the globe (longitude) decides when a place faces the Sun

questions.q: Riya's globe shows the grid of parallels and meridians. She wants a pair of lines that crosses at exactly one point, so that the crossing could mark a single place. Which pair should she choose?
questions.a: A parallel such as 20°N is a circle running east and west, and a meridian is a half-circle from pole to pole, so they cross only once. Two parallels never meet; two meridians meet at both poles; the Equator is itself a parallel, so it never meets another parallel.
o: The Equator and the parallel of 20°N

questions.q:
Riya flies over Kenya exactly where her globe shows the Equator and sees no line on the ground. Her brother says: 'So the lines on a globe are made up, and a position given by them cannot be trusted.'
(a) What does Riya's view from the plane tell you about the Equator?
(b) Explain why her brother's conclusion does not follow from (a).
questions.a: (a) The Equator, like the other parallels and meridians, is an imaginary line: it is drawn on the globe, not marked on the Earth. (b) Being imaginary does not make the lines useless. Together they form a grid, and each place gets two coordinates, its latitude and longitude, measured from fixed references (the Equator, halfway between the poles, and the Prime Meridian). Those two numbers fix the place precisely whether or not anything is painted on the ground.
s: Part (a): the Equator is an imaginary line drawn only on the globe
Part (b): imaginary lines still form a grid of two coordinates that fixes a place precisely

questions.q:
On a classroom globe, a tape laid along the surface from the North Pole to the South Pole measures 64 cm.
(a) How far from the North Pole, along the tape, must the Equator be drawn? Why?
(b) A sticker sits on the tape 16 cm from the South Pole. Is it in the Northern or the Southern Hemisphere, and how far is it from the Equator along the tape?
questions.a: (a) 32 cm: the Equator lies halfway between the two poles, and 64 / 2 = 32. (b) Southern Hemisphere: it is 16 cm from the South Pole, which is less than the 32 cm to the Equator, so it lies between the Equator and the South Pole, 32 - 16 = 16 cm from the Equator.
s: Part (a): 32 cm, halfway between the poles
Part (b): Southern Hemisphere, 16 cm from the Equator

questions.q: On a flat world map, a large island near the North Pole looks about as big as India. On a globe of the Earth it looks much smaller. Which is the better guide to the island's real size, and why?
questions.a: The globe: it has the same spherical shape as the Earth, while a sphere's surface cannot be represented accurately on a flat sheet. A flat map is not wrong everywhere, but it must stretch or tear the round surface somewhere. Being printed later or showing more names does not make a map more accurate.
o: The globe, since it has the same round shape as the real Earth
The flat map, since it shows the island and India side by side
The flat map, since it is drawn with a scale and a north arrow
Neither, since sizes can never be compared on any Earth model

questions.q: Sana says: 'The Equator on my globe is just a line someone decided to draw, so it could have been drawn round the globe anywhere, as long as it makes a full circle.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. It is true that the Equator is an imaginary line drawn on the globe, but its place is not a matter of choice. The poles are the two points that stay fixed as the globe spins, and the Equator is the circle exactly halfway between them. A circle drawn anywhere else would not be halfway between the poles, so it would not be the Equator.
s: Verdict: No
The poles are fixed by the spin
The Equator must lie halfway between them, so its place is fixed

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Because the Earth is slightly flattened at the poles, a perfectly round globe is of no use for studying it.
2. A globe made of cardboard can still show the Earth's geography.
3. A globe shows the shapes of the continents more truly than a flat world map, because it has the same shape as the Earth.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 are correct: globes are generally made of metal, plastic or cardboard, and the globe shares the Earth's spherical shape. 1 is false: the flattening is slight, so in practice the Earth is considered spherical and a round globe represents it well.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A globe represents the geography of the Earth better than a flat map.
Reason (R): The Earth is a perfect sphere, with no flattening anywhere on it.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true: the globe and the Earth share the same spherical shape. R is false: the Earth is nearly a sphere but slightly flattened at the poles.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: In a dark room a desk lamp shines on a globe that is turned slowly eastward. At one moment India's side is lit while the Americas are in shadow. What does this model show?
questions.a: At one and the same moment it is daytime in some places and night in others, which is why the time differs from place to place. The lamp stays fixed, so it does not show the Sun moving; it shows times differ, not that they are the same.
o: At one moment it is day in some places, night in others
The Sun travels all the way round the Earth once every day
It is the same time of day at every place on the Earth
Only places close to the poles are ever left in shadow

questions.q: True or False? 'On a globe spinning on its stand, the North Pole stays in one place while the countries along the Equator move past you.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The poles are the fixed points at the top and bottom of a spinning globe; the Equator lies halfway between them, so the places along it move round as the globe turns.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the poles are the fixed points of the spin; places on the Equator move round

questions.q:
A school in Jaipur can buy only one item this year for its geography room: a plastic globe of the Earth with grid lines, or a set of large flat wall maps (world, India and Rajasthan). The school already owns a small atlas with maps of the world, India and every State. The wall maps can be seen by all 40 students at once; the globe is small, so only a few students can gather round it at a time. In term 1, Class 6 will study the Earth's shape and how latitude and longitude locate places; in term 2 they will read and draw maps of their own locality. The headmistress's rule: buy the item whose job cannot be done at all, even slowly, with what the school already has.
(a) Why does term 1's work on the Earth's shape need a sphere rather than a flat map?
(b) The wall-map set includes a large world map. Why does buying it not remove the problem in (a)?
(c) What real advantage do the wall maps have over the atlas, and could the atlas still do their job, though less conveniently?
(d) Apply the headmistress's rule and decide which item to buy, stating the cost the school accepts.
questions.a: (a) The Earth is nearly a sphere, and a sphere cannot be represented accurately on a flat sheet; the globe has the same shape as the Earth. (b) A large world map is still flat, so it carries the same problem as the atlas's world map; size does not help. (c) The whole class can see a wall map at once, while the atlas must be passed round or shared; but the atlas holds the same world, India and State maps, so it can still do the job, only more slowly. (d) The globe: no flat map the school owns or could buy can show the Earth's shape truly, while the wall maps' job can be done, less conveniently, with the atlas. The cost is that only a few students can use the globe at a time, so the class must take turns in groups.
s: Part (a): a sphere cannot be shown accurately on a flat sheet
Part (b): a bigger flat map is still flat
Part (c): whole-class viewing at once; the atlas can still do the job more slowly
Part (d): the globe under the rule, accepting that students must take turns

questions.q:
A science centre sells a sphere showing the craters and plains of the Moon, with a grid of lines on it.
(a) Why is it a globe even though it shows no country?
(b) How could its grid help two visitors talk about the same crater?
(c) A visitor says the sphere must be inaccurate because astronauts saw no such lines on the real Moon. Reply to him.
questions.a: (a) A globe is any sphere on which a map is drawn; the map may be of the Earth, the Moon, Mars or the sky. (b) The grid gives each spot two coordinates, so a visitor can name the crater's position precisely and the other can find it, as with the stationery shop's row and number. (c) The lines are imaginary: they are drawn on the globe to make the grid, not marked on the surface, so not seeing them on the real Moon says nothing about the sphere's accuracy.
s: Part (a): a sphere with a map drawn on it is a globe
Part (b): two coordinates fix the crater precisely
Part (c): the grid lines are imaginary, drawn only on the globe

questions.q: A student writes: 'North Pole: latitude 90°. South Pole: latitude 90°. So both poles have the same latitude.' Point out the error and explain why it matters.
questions.a: The letters are missing: the North Pole is 90°N and the South Pole is 90°S. Both are 90 degrees from the Equator, but on opposite sides, so they are the two places on Earth farthest apart in latitude, not the same latitude.
s: Error: N and S are missing; 90°N and 90°S
Why it matters: same distance from the Equator but on opposite sides

questions.q: Four weather stations lie at 35°S, 10°N, 60°N and 75°S. Using the link between latitude and climate, which list ranks them from the warmest expected climate to the coldest?
questions.a: Climate grows colder as latitude increases, that is, with distance from the Equator, whichever hemisphere the place is in: 10 degrees, then 35, 60 and 75. Ranking south latitudes as colder or warmer just because they are south, or ordering by the hemisphere first, ignores that rule.

questions.q: A ship's log records its latitude at noon each day: 12°N, 6°N, 0°, 6°S, 12°S. A student reads it and says the ship's latitude fell all week. What is the correct reading of the log?
questions.a: The ship sailed steadily south all week. Its latitude, its distance from the Equator, fell from 12 to 0 and then rose again to 12, now with S. South latitudes are not below zero; they are distances on the other side of the Equator.
o: It fell to 0° and then rose, as the ship kept sailing south
It fell all week, because south latitudes count below zero
It rose all week, because the ship was nearing the South Pole
It stayed the same, because the ship kept to one meridian

questions.q: India's latitudes extend from about 8°N to about 37°N, so the country stretches across roughly ___ degrees of latitude.
A research station in the Southern Hemisphere is twice as far, in degrees of latitude, from the South Pole as it is from the Equator. What is its latitude?
questions.a: If it is x degrees from the Equator, it is 90 - x degrees from the South Pole, and 90 - x = 2x gives x = 30, so 30°S. 60°S has the two distances the wrong way round; 45°S is the halfway point; 30°N is in the wrong hemisphere.

questions.q:
Read this page from a student's travel blog.
'Day 1: We set off from a port on the Equator. Day 4: We reached latitude 45°N. The parallel we were on was a bigger circle than the Equator, and the air was hotter than on Day 1. Day 9: We reached a spot only 5 degrees of latitude from the North Pole.'
(a) What was the latitude on Day 9?
(b) Find the two mistakes in the Day 4 entry and correct them.
(c) How many degrees of latitude did the group move from Day 4 to Day 9, and what change in climate should they have noticed?
questions.a: (a) 90 - 5 = 85°N. (b) The 45°N parallel is a smaller circle than the Equator, which is the largest; and moving away from the Equator the climate becomes more moderate, not hotter. (c) 85 - 45 = 40 degrees; the climate should have grown colder (frigid) closer to the pole.
s: Part (a): 85°N
Part (b): the parallel is smaller, not bigger; the climate is more moderate, not hotter
Part (c): 40 degrees, growing colder towards the pole

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A place at 70°S generally has a colder climate than a place at 10°N.
Reason (R): The climate grows colder as latitude increases, that is, as one moves away from the Equator towards either pole.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A. 70°S is 70 degrees from the Equator and 10°N only 10, so by the rule in R the place at 70°S is the colder one; being in the south is not itself the reason.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: 'Latitude tells you something about a place's climate, but it cannot by itself tell you exactly where the place is.' Do you agree? Support your view with the meaning of latitude, its link to climate and an example.
questions.a: Latitude is the distance of a place from the Equator, in degrees, towards a pole, from 0° to 90°N or 90°S. Latitude is linked to climate: around the Equator the climate is generally hot (torrid), it grows moderate (temperate) as latitude increases, and colder (frigid) near the poles. So a latitude hints at the kind of climate. But a parallel of latitude is a whole circle around the Earth; every place on that circle has the same latitude, for example many places share Delhi's 29°N. To fix one point a second coordinate is needed, longitude.
s: Meaning of latitude: distance from the Equator in degrees
Climate link: torrid, temperate, frigid as latitude increases
A parallel is a full circle, so many places share one latitude
An example such as places sharing 29°N
Conclusion: a second coordinate, longitude, is needed to fix the place

questions.q: Compare the chessboard's way of naming squares with the way places are located on a globe. (a) What do the letters and numbers of the chessboard do? (b) Which measure on the globe plays the part of one of them, and what does it measure? (c) Give one way the globe's lines differ from the chessboard's.
questions.a: (a) The letters a to h and numbers 1 to 8 are two coordinates that mark each square precisely. (b) Latitude is one coordinate: the distance of a place from the Equator, in degrees, towards a pole (longitude is the other). (c) The parallels of latitude are circles that grow smaller towards the poles, while the chessboard's rows are all the same length.
s: Part (a): two coordinates fix each square precisely
Part (b): latitude, the distance from the Equator in degrees
Part (c): parallels shrink towards the poles, chessboard rows do not

questions.q: Asha texts a friend: 'Meet me in the 4th row of the cloth market.' The rows are long, with many shops of the same size. Why might the friend fail to find her, and what would fix it?
questions.a: One coordinate is missing; add the number of the shop in the row, as in '7th shop in the 5th row'. The meeting time is not a coordinate of place; rows can be counted; degrees are for the Earth, not a market.
o: One coordinate is missing; add the number of the shop in the row
Rows cannot be counted, so she must give the name of the shop
She must add the time of meeting, which is the second coordinate
She must give the row in degrees, as is done for places on Earth

questions.q:
A research ship sails due north from 10°S, across the Equator, to 80°N.
(a) How many degrees of latitude does it cover in all?
(b) At what latitude is it when it has covered exactly half of that distance?
(c) Using (b), is the parallel it is on at that halfway point larger or smaller than the parallel it started on? Explain.
(d) At which point of the whole voyage was it on the largest parallel?
(e) The captain writes: 'At the end we are eight times as far from the Equator as at the start, so the parallel we are on is eight times smaller.' Judge each half of his sentence.
questions.a: (a) 10 + 80 = 90 degrees. (b) Half of 90 is 45 degrees; 10 of them bring it to the Equator, and 35 more take it to 35°N. (c) Smaller: at the start it was 10 degrees from the Equator, at 35°N it is 35 degrees away, and parallels grow smaller as one moves away from the Equator towards a pole. (d) At the Equator, the largest parallel. (e) The first half is right: 80 degrees is eight times 10 degrees. The second half does not follow: we only know that parallels grow smaller towards the poles, not that they shrink in the same proportion as the latitude grows.
s: Part (a): 90 degrees
Part (b): 35°N
Part (c): smaller, because it is farther from the Equator
Part (d): at the Equator
Part (e): first half right (80 = 8 x 10); second half does not follow

questions.q: Rohan says: 'If I keep walking from the Equator towards the South Pole, my latitude keeps increasing, and broadly the climate around me changes from hot to moderate to cold.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. Latitude measures distance from the Equator towards a pole, so walking south from 0° it rises towards 90°S. Climate follows latitude: generally hot (torrid) near the Equator, more moderate (temperate) as latitude increases, colder (frigid) near the pole. The south follows the same pattern as the north.
s: Verdict: yes
Latitude increases from 0° towards 90°S as he walks
Climate goes torrid to temperate to frigid as latitude increases

questions.q:
Tara traces the parallel of 40°N on a globe with her finger.
(a) In which directions does her finger move?
(b) She then traces the parallel of 70°N. How will this circle compare in size with the first, and why?
questions.a: (a) East and west, parallel to the Equator. (b) It will be a smaller circle, because the parallels of latitude grow smaller as one moves northward towards the pole.
s: Part (a): east and west, parallel to the Equator
Part (b): smaller, since parallels shrink towards the poles

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. The Equator is itself a parallel of latitude, and the largest one.
2. A place at 60°N is farther from the Equator than a place at 25°S.
3. Every parallel of latitude runs east and west.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: All three are correct. The Equator is the largest of the latitude circles; latitude measures distance from the Equator, so 60 degrees is farther than 25 degrees whichever side; parallels run east and west, parallel to the Equator.

questions.q: On a globe, Ritu traces the parallel of 20°N eastward all the way round, and Sam traces the parallel of 60°N all the way round. Which statement about their two paths is correct?
questions.a: Ritu's path is longer, because the parallels grow smaller towards the poles and 20°N is nearer the Equator; and since a parallel runs east and west, every point on it keeps the same latitude, so neither latitude changes. Sam's circle is the smaller one; moving east does not raise latitude.
o: Ritu's path is longer; neither latitude changes
Sam's path is longer; neither latitude changes
The paths are equal; both latitudes rise eastward
Ritu's path is longer; her latitude rises eastward

questions.q:
Ravi walks south from a village at 10°S to a town at 30°S.
(a) Is his latitude increasing or decreasing? Explain.
(b) Ravi's friend says, 'Latitude always increases as you go north.' Use (a) to correct her.
questions.a: (a) Increasing, from 10 to 30 degrees, because he is moving farther from the Equator. (b) Latitude measures distance from the Equator, so it increases moving away from the Equator in either direction, north or south. Going north from 30°S it would actually decrease until the Equator.
s: Part (a): increasing, as he moves away from the Equator
Part (b): latitude grows away from the Equator both ways, so north is not always an increase

questions.q:
A globe has parallels drawn every 15 degrees, starting from the Equator, towards each pole. The poles themselves are points, not circles.
(a) How many parallel circles, including the Equator, does the globe show?
(b) Which parallel on it is exactly the same size as the parallel of 30°N? Explain.
questions.a: (a) North: 15°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 75° (90°N is the pole, a point), so 5; the same 5 in the south; plus the Equator: 5 + 5 + 1 = 11. (b) 30°S. Parallels shrink in the same way going north or south from the Equator, so the two parallels 30 degrees from it on either side are the same size.
s: Part (a): 11 circles
Part (b): 30°S, the same distance from the Equator on the other side

questions.q:
Match each place in Column A with its latitude in Column B.
Column A: 1. a ship exactly halfway between the two poles  2. an explorer at the southern point that stays fixed as the Earth spins  3. a town 8 degrees south of India's northern limit of 37°N  4. a town 16 degrees south of the town in 3
Column B: a. 90°S  b. 0°  c. 13°N  d. 29°N
questions.a: Halfway between the poles is the Equator, 0°. The southern fixed point is the South Pole, 90°S. 37 - 8 = 29°N. 29 - 16 = 13°N.

questions.q: True or False? 'Latitude tells how far a place is from the North Pole, so a town at 20°N is 20 degrees from the pole.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Latitude measures the distance from the Equator, which is 0°, towards a pole at 90°. A town at 20°N is 20 degrees from the Equator and 90 - 20 = 70 degrees from the North Pole.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: latitude is measured from the Equator; 20°N is 70 degrees from the pole

questions.q:
A company plans to test equipment at four weather stations.
| Station | Latitude |
| K | 0° |
| L | 30°N |
| M | 60°S |
| N | 88°N |
Its supply ship cannot sail beyond 70° of latitude, north or south.
(a) Which station lies on the longest parallel?
(b) Which station is farthest from the Equator, and how far is it from its pole?
(c) Rank the stations from the warmest expected climate to the coldest, using the link between latitude and climate.
(d) A battery must be tested at the coldest station the ship can supply. Which station should the company choose? Justify using (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) K, on the Equator, the largest parallel. (b) N, at 88°N, only 90 - 88 = 2 degrees from the North Pole. (c) K (0°), L (30°N), M (60°S), N (88°N): the climate grows colder as latitude increases. (d) M. N would be the coldest, but at 88° it lies beyond the ship's 70° limit; M at 60° is within the limit and is the coldest of the stations the ship can reach.
s: Part (a): K
Part (b): N, 2 degrees from the pole
Part (c): K, L, M, N
Part (d): M, since N is beyond the 70° limit

questions.q: A student reasons: 'If I start on the Equator and travel 100 degrees of latitude due north, I will reach latitude 100°N.' Show that this cannot happen, and find the latitude where the student actually ends up.
questions.a: Latitude measures distance from the Equator, 0°, and the North Pole is 90°N, the farthest point north. After 90 degrees the student is at the pole; from there every direction is south, so the last 10 degrees take the student down the other side of the globe, back towards the Equator. The student ends at 90 - 10 = 80°N, and no place can have a latitude above 90°.
s: Latitude is measured from the Equator; the pole at 90°N is the farthest point north
Beyond the pole every direction is south, so latitude starts to fall
The student ends at 80°N; 100°N is impossible

questions.q: Farhan says: 'Two towns with exactly the same latitude must be close to each other, because they lie on the same parallel.' Is he right? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. A parallel of latitude is a whole circle running east and west around the Earth. Two towns on it are the same distance from the Equator, but they can be anywhere along that circle, even on opposite sides of the Earth. To tell how close they are, their longitudes are needed too.
s: Verdict: No
A parallel is a full circle round the Earth
Same latitude only means the same distance from the Equator; longitude decides how far apart

questions.q:
A coastguard chart shows three boats: P at 12°N, 30°E; Q at 5°S, 30°W; R at 40°S, 100°E.
(a) Which boat is in both the Southern and the Western Hemispheres?
(b) Which two boats are the same distance from the Prime Meridian? Are they on the same side of it?
(c) Boat P sails due west along its parallel until it reaches Boat Q's meridian. How many degrees of longitude does it cross, which line does it pass, and what is its latitude at the end?
questions.a: (a) Q: S puts it south of the Equator and W puts it west of the Prime Meridian. (b) P and Q, each 30 degrees from the Prime Meridian, but on opposite sides (P east, Q west). (c) 30 degrees to reach the Prime Meridian and 30 more beyond it, so 60 degrees; it passes the Prime Meridian (0°); sailing along a parallel does not change latitude, so it is still at 12°N.
s: Part (a): Q
Part (b): P and Q, 30 degrees each, on opposite sides
Part (c): 60 degrees across the Prime Meridian, still 12°N

questions.q: Using round figures, New York is at 74°W and Delhi at 77°E. How many degrees of longitude separate them, measured across the Prime Meridian?
questions.a: They are on opposite sides of the Prime Meridian, so the degrees add: 74 + 77 = 151. 3 subtracts two values on opposite sides; 103 is 180 - 77; 180 assumes they are opposite each other.

questions.q:
A quiz card says: 'Two towns are both at 77°E, but one is in the Northern Hemisphere and the other in the Southern Hemisphere.'
(a) Is this possible? Explain using the shape of a meridian.
(b) What do the two towns have in common, and what must differ between their coordinates?
questions.a: (a) Yes. A meridian is a half-circle running from the North Pole to the South Pole, so it crosses the Equator and passes through both hemispheres. (b) They share the same longitude (they are on the same meridian, the same distance east of the Prime Meridian); their latitudes must differ, one marked N and the other S.
s: Part (a): yes, a meridian runs pole to pole across the Equator
Part (b): same longitude, different latitudes (N and S)

questions.q:
Three towns: A at 20°N, 10°E; B at 20°N, 150°W; C at 70°N, 10°E.
(a) Which two towns would the link between latitude and climate expect to have broadly the same kind of climate?
(b) Towns A and B are 160 degrees of longitude apart. Why does this not change your answer to (a)?
questions.a: (a) A and B, because they are at the same latitude, the same distance from the Equator. (b) The climate link is with latitude, the distance from the Equator. Longitude measures distance east or west of the Prime Meridian and tells us about time, not about how far a place is from the Equator. (C shares A's longitude but is much nearer the pole.)
s: Part (a): A and B, the same latitude
Part (b): climate goes with latitude; longitude tells east-west position and time

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Ujjayini meridian became a reference for calculations in all Indian astronomical texts.
Reason (R): Measuring longitude required accurate timekeeping, which was not as precise in ancient times as it is today.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but R does not explain A. R explains something else: why some cities the old texts place on the Ujjayini meridian lie a little away from it. It gives no reason why the meridian became the reference.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? 'A buoy floating at 0° latitude and 180° longitude lies where the Equator crosses the Prime Meridian.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. 0° latitude is the Equator, but the Prime Meridian is 0° longitude. 180° is the meridian on the opposite side of the Earth from it (near the International Date Line), so the buoy is on the Equator half-way round the globe from where it meets the Prime Meridian.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: 180° is opposite the Prime Meridian (0°); the buoy is on the Equator, half-way round from that crossing

questions.q:
A pilot starts at 30°W on the Equator and flies eastward along the Equator in three legs, each of 120 degrees of longitude.
(a) What is her longitude at the end of the first leg, and which line did she cross on it?
(b) What is her longitude at the end of the second leg? Show how you handle passing 180°.
(c) Using (b), where is she at the end of the third leg?
(d) In which hemisphere (east or west) is she at the end of each leg?
(e) Her co-pilot says, 'Since we always flew east, the number in our longitude kept going up.' Judge this, using your answers.
questions.a: (a) 30 degrees bring her to the Prime Meridian and 90 more take her to 90°E; she crossed the Prime Meridian (0°). (b) From 90°E, 90 degrees take her to 180°, and the remaining 30 degrees carry her into west longitudes: 180 - 30 = 150°W. (c) From 150°W, 120 degrees east brings her to 30°W, back at the start (3 x 120 = 360). (d) Eastern after the first leg; Western after the second and third. (e) Wrong: the number rose from 0° to 180° while she was in east longitudes, but after 180° the longitude is marked W and the number fell, from 180°W down to 30°W.
s: Part (a): 90°E, crossing the Prime Meridian
Part (b): 150°W after passing 180°
Part (c): 30°W, back at the start
Part (d): Eastern, then Western, Western
Part (e): rejects the claim; W values fall after 180°

questions.q:
A quiz answer gives a town's position as 77°N, 29°E and says the town is in India. India's latitudes run from about 8°N to 37°N and its longitudes from about 68°E to 97°E.
(a) Show that the town cannot be in India.
(b) What mistake was most probably made, and what was the correct position likely to be?
questions.a: (a) 77°N is far north of India's limit of 37°N, and 29°E is far west of its limit of 68°E, so the position lies outside both ranges. (b) The two numbers were swapped: the latitude was written as the longitude and the other way round. The likely position is 29°N, 77°E, which fits both ranges (it is Delhi's position in round figures).
s: Part (a): 77°N and 29°E both fall outside India's ranges
Part (b): the values were swapped; 29°N, 77°E

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. A place at 100°E is farther from the Prime Meridian, in degrees of longitude, than a place at 80°W.
2. Like parallels of latitude, meridians of longitude grow shorter as they get closer to the poles.
3. 180°E and 180°W are the same meridian, written simply as 180°.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are correct: longitude is the distance from the Prime Meridian, so 100 degrees is farther than 80 whichever side; and 180°E and 180°W coincide. 2 is false: every meridian is a half-circle from pole to pole, all of the same length; it is the parallels that shrink.

questions.q:
Match each event in Column A with the line in Column B.
Column A: 1. A ship crossing this line passes from the Northern into the Southern Hemisphere  2. A plane crossing this line at 0° passes from the Western into the Eastern Hemisphere  3. Ancient astronomers' texts used this 'middle line' for calculations  4. 180°E and 180°W are two names for this one meridian
Column B: a. 180°  b. the Equator  c. the Prime Meridian  d. madhya rekha
questions.a: The Equator divides north and south; the Prime Meridian at 0° divides west and east; madhya rekha, the 'middle line' through Ujjayini, was the astronomers' reference; 180°E and 180°W are the same meridian, written 180°.

questions.q:
(a) Along which line, and starting from which meridian, is longitude measured?
(b) Using (a), explain why no place can have a longitude greater than 180°.
questions.a: (a) Along the Equator, eastward or westward from the Prime Meridian (0°). (b) Going 180 degrees east brings you to the meridian opposite the Prime Meridian, which is also 180°W. Going any farther you are now nearer the Prime Meridian from the west, so the longitude starts falling as a west value; 180° is the largest.
s: Part (a): along the Equator, east or west from the Prime Meridian
Part (b): 180°E and 180°W meet at the opposite meridian, so values beyond fall back

questions.q: Kiran traces two meridians on a globe from the North Pole to the South Pole, one passing through Africa and one through Asia. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Meridians are half-circles running from pole to pole, and the shortest pole-to-pole line is the same length whichever continent it crosses. They are not full circles that shrink (that describes parallels), and they all meet at the poles.
o: Both are half-circles of equal length meeting at the poles
The one through Asia is longer, as Asia is a bigger continent
Both are full circles that grow smaller towards the poles
They never meet, since all meridians are parallel lines

questions.q: Write a pair of coordinates for an imaginary island that is in the Southern and the Western Hemispheres and is nearer to the 180° meridian than to the Prime Meridian. Then show how you checked each condition.
questions.a: Any pair with latitude marked S and longitude marked W of more than 90°, for example 20°S, 150°W. Check: S places it south of the Equator; W places it west of the Prime Meridian; 150°W is 150 degrees from the Prime Meridian but only 180 - 150 = 30 degrees from the 180° meridian.
s: A latitude marked S
A longitude marked W
Longitude above 90°W, with the distance to 180° checked

questions.q:
A museum guide in Ujjain says: 'The madhya rekha was a prime meridian, so it did exactly the same job as the Greenwich Meridian does today.'
(a) What job does a prime meridian do when longitudes are measured?
(b) Through which city did the madhya rekha pass, and what is its longitude on today's grid, to one decimal place?
(c) Using (b) and 15 degrees per hour, find how many degrees and about how many hours and minutes of local time separate the madhya rekha from Greenwich.
(d) Some ancient cities that old texts place on the madhya rekha lie a little off it on a modern map. Why, and what does that say about the old reference compared with today's?
(e) Judge the guide's claim, taking 'the same job' to mean a zero line that all its users measure from and that is equally precise.
questions.a: (a) It is the reference line, 0° longitude, from which longitude is measured east or west along the Equator. (b) Ujjayini, today Ujjain; about 75.8°E. (c) 75.8 degrees; 75.8 / 15 = about 5.05 hours, that is about 5 hours 3 minutes (75.8 x 4 = 303.2 minutes). (d) Measuring longitude needed accurate timekeeping, which was not as precise then; so the old reference was used with less precision than today's. (e) Partly right. For its users it did the same job: Indian astronomers knew the need for a zero meridian, and the Ujjayini meridian was the reference for calculations in all Indian astronomical texts. But its users were Indian astronomers, not the world: Greenwich became the international standard only when some nations agreed in 1884. And by (d) its placings were less precise. So it meets the first part of the test, not the 'all users' scope of today's line, and not the precision.
s: Part (a): the 0° reference from which longitude is measured
Part (b): Ujjain, about 75.8°E
Part (c): 75.8 degrees, about 5 h 3 min
Part (d): less accurate timekeeping, so less precise placings
Part (e): partly right; a zero line for all Indian astronomical texts, but not international (1884) and less precise

questions.q: An explorer stands exactly at the North Pole. Her friend asks for her longitude. Which reply is correct?
questions.a: All the meridians are half-circles that meet at the poles, so every meridian passes through the point where she stands; no single longitude belongs to her. Her latitude, 90°N, is what fixes her position. 0° and 180° are just two of the many meridians that meet there.
o: All meridians meet there, so no single longitude fits
It is 0°, because the Prime Meridian starts at the pole
It is 180°, because the pole is opposite the Equator
It is 90°E, because the pole lies at 90 degrees

questions.q:
A research vessel on the Equator at 170°E must refuel at one of two ports, also on the Equator: Port X at 160°W or Port Y at 130°E. It has fuel for at most 45 degrees of longitude. A storm blocks the stretch of sea between 175°E and 175°W.
(a) How many degrees of longitude is Port X, sailing eastward?
(b) How many degrees is Port Y, sailing westward?
(c) Which line would the eastward route to Port X cross, and how is the longitude written on that line?
(d) Which port should the captain choose? Justify using (a)-(c).
questions.a: (a) 10 degrees to 180° and 20 more to 160°W: 30 degrees. (b) 170 - 130 = 40 degrees. (c) The 180° meridian, written 180° without E or W, since 180°E and 180°W are the same line. (d) Port Y. Port X is nearer (30 degrees), but the only short route to it crosses 180°, inside the storm zone; the westward route to X would be 170 + 160 = 330 degrees, far beyond the fuel. Port Y is 40 degrees away, within the 45-degree limit and clear of the storm.
s: Part (a): 30 degrees
Part (b): 40 degrees
Part (c): the 180° meridian, written without E or W
Part (d): Port Y, since the short route to X is in the storm and the long one exceeds the fuel

questions.q: Using round figures, Delhi is at 77°E and Tokyo at 140°E, so Tokyo lies ___ degrees of longitude east of Delhi.
Using round figures, Tokyo is at 140°E and New York at 74°W. A plane flies from Tokyo eastward over the Pacific, crossing the 180° meridian, to New York. How many degrees of longitude does it cross?
questions.a: 146: 180 - 140 = 40 degrees to reach 180°, then 180 - 74 = 106 degrees to New York; 40 + 106 = 146. 214 is the westward route across the Prime Meridian (140 + 74); 66 subtracts the two numbers; 34 adds and takes the total from 180.

questions.q: India's latitudes extend from about 8°N to 37°N and its longitudes from about 68°E to 97°E. Which of these positions could be a place in India?
questions.a: 23°N, 88°E lies inside both ranges. 23°S is south of the Equator; 88°W is west of the Prime Meridian; 40°N is north of India's 37°N limit.

questions.q:
A museum in Ujjain is making a panel. Its facts sheet says: the Ujjayini meridian is at about 75.8°E; Delhi is at about 77°E; India's longitudes extend from about 68°E to 97°E.
(a) How many degrees east of the Ujjayini meridian is Delhi?
(b) How far is the Ujjayini meridian from India's western limit, and how far from its eastern limit?
(c) Which longitude is exactly midway between India's western and eastern limits?
(d) The designer wants the caption 'This line runs through the exact middle of India from west to east.' Should the museum accept it? Use (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) 77 - 75.8 = 1.2 degrees. (b) 75.8 - 68 = 7.8 degrees from the western limit; 97 - 75.8 = 21.2 degrees from the eastern limit. (c) (68 + 97) / 2 = 82.5°E. (d) No: the line is 6.7 degrees west of the midway longitude and much nearer the western limit (7.8) than the eastern (21.2), so the caption would be wrong for today's India.
s: Part (a): 1.2 degrees
Part (b): 7.8 and 21.2 degrees
Part (c): 82.5°E
Part (d): reject the caption; the line is 6.7 degrees west of the midpoint

questions.q: Neha says: 'Greenwich was chosen as the international Prime Meridian in 1884, and it was the first prime meridian anyone ever used.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. The first half is true: in 1884 some nations decided that the meridian through Greenwich would be the international standard for the Prime Meridian. The second half is wrong: Greenwich was not the first prime meridian; many centuries before Europe, India had its own, the madhya rekha through Ujjayini, used in all Indian astronomical texts.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: Greenwich became the international standard in 1884
Wrong part: it was not the first; India's Ujjayini meridian came many centuries earlier

questions.q: A cricket match begins at 12 noon local time at a ground on the Prime Meridian. What is the local time at that moment in a town at 45°W?
questions.a: 45 / 15 = 3 hours, and places west of the Prime Meridian are behind, so 12 noon - 3 hours = 9 am. 3 pm adds instead of subtracting; 11 am and 10 am are the times at 15°W and 30°W.

questions.q:
A news channel in Kolkata shows two clocks on screen: 'London (GMT) 9:00 am' and 'India 2:30 pm'.
(a) By how much is the India clock ahead, and does this agree with how Indian Standard Time is defined?
(b) The Earth turns 15 degrees every hour. Work out how many degrees east of Greenwich a meridian must lie for its time to be 5 hours 30 minutes ahead.
(c) India's longitudes run from about 68°E to 97°E. Does the meridian from (b) pass through India, and why does that matter for a standard time?
questions.a: (a) 2:30 pm - 9:00 am = 5 hours 30 minutes, which agrees: IST is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT. (b) 5.5 x 15 = 82.5 degrees, so 82.5°E (this figure is worked out, not given). (c) Yes, 82.5°E lies between 68°E and 97°E. That matters because a country bases its standard time on a meridian passing through it.
s: Part (a): 5 h 30 min ahead, matching IST
Part (c): inside 68°E-97°E; standard time uses a meridian through the country

questions.q: A football final in a city at 45°W kicks off at 3 pm local time. Local time changes by one hour for every 15 degrees of longitude. What is the local time then in a town at 30°E?
questions.a: The two places are 45 + 30 = 75 degrees apart, and 75 / 15 = 5 hours; the town lies to the east, where the local time is ahead, so 3 pm + 5 h = 8 pm. 10 am goes the wrong way; 4 pm uses 45 - 30 = 15 degrees; 6 pm counts only the 45 degrees to Greenwich.

questions.q: An imaginary country stretches from 60°E to 90°E. Its standard time is based on the meridian exactly in the middle of the country. At a town on its eastern edge, how does the local time compare with the clocks?
questions.a: The middle meridian is (60 + 90) / 2 = 75°E. The eastern edge, 90°E, is 15 degrees east of it, which is 1 hour, and local time is ahead towards the east, so local time there is 1 hour ahead of the clocks. 'Behind' reverses the direction; 2 hours uses the country's full width; 'no difference' confuses standard time with local time.
o: Local time is 1 hour ahead of the clocks
Local time is 1 hour behind the clocks
Local time is 2 hours ahead of the clocks
There is no difference under one standard time

questions.q: Imran says: 'All the clocks in the world should show the same time at the same moment, because a day is 24 hours long everywhere.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: No. The day is 24 hours long everywhere, but the Earth spins from west to east, turning 15 degrees every hour, so places face the Sun at different moments: when it is breakfast time in one country it is lunchtime in another. Local time is one hour ahead for every 15 degrees east and one hour behind for every 15 degrees west: at noon at Greenwich it is 1 pm at 15°E and 11 am at 15°W, and 5:30 pm by IST in India.
s: Verdict: No
The Earth's spin means places face the Sun at different times
An example: 1 pm at 15°E, 11 am at 15°W, or 5:30 pm IST

questions.q: Local time changes by 4 minutes for each degree of longitude. When it is noon at Greenwich, what is the local time at a town at 77°E?
questions.a: 77 x 4 = 308 minutes = 5 hours 8 minutes ahead, so 5:08 pm. 5:30 pm is IST, not local time; 5:13 pm misreads 77/15 = 5.13 hours as 5 h 13 min; 6:52 am subtracts instead of adding.

questions.q: Pooja claims that two towns in the same country, 30 degrees of longitude apart, can have exactly the same local time, because their clocks show the same time. Show that their local times cannot be the same, and explain why their clocks may still agree.
questions.a: Local time depends on longitude: 30 / 15 = 2 hours, so the eastern town's local time is 2 hours ahead of the western town's; equal local times are impossible. Their clocks may still agree because the country uses one standard time, based on a single meridian, for convenience; the clocks show standard time, not local time.
s: 30 degrees means 2 hours of local time difference
So the local times cannot be equal; the eastern town is ahead
Clocks agree because they show the country's standard time, not local time

questions.q:
A graph of time zones shows longitudes from 45°W to 45°E along the bottom, and local times along the top with 12 PM over 0°. Each coloured zone is 15 degrees wide and centred on a meridian.
(a) Between which longitudes does the zone centred on 30°E run?
(b) What local time does the graph show for that zone?
questions.a: (a) 15 degrees wide and centred on 30°E, so from 22.5°E to 37.5°E. (b) 30 / 15 = 2 hours ahead of noon: 2 PM.
s: Part (a): 22.5°E to 37.5°E
Part (b): 2 PM

questions.q:
A ship carries a clock set to Greenwich time. On a certain day it is mid-day (12 noon local time) on the ship when that clock reads 2 pm.
(a) Is the ship east or west of the Prime Meridian? Explain.
(b) Using (a), what is the ship's longitude?
questions.a: (a) West: the ship's local time (noon) is behind Greenwich (2 pm), and local time falls behind going westward. (b) 2 hours x 15 degrees = 30 degrees, so 30°W.
s: Part (a): west, because local time is behind Greenwich
Part (b): 2 x 15 = 30, so 30°W

questions.q:
A flight leaves Delhi at 10:00 pm IST and lands in London after 9 hours in the air. Take London's time to be GMT.
(a) What is the GMT time when the flight leaves Delhi?
(b) Using (a), what is the GMT time when it lands?
(c) What time is it then by IST?
(d) On which day, compared with the departure day, does it land?
(e) The passenger's family in Delhi gets up at 7:30 am IST. She wants to phone them as soon as they are up. How long after landing should she call, and what will London clocks show then?
questions.a: (a) 10:00 pm - 5 h 30 min = 4:30 pm GMT. (b) 4:30 pm + 9 hours = 1:30 am GMT. (c) 1:30 am + 5 h 30 min = 7:00 am IST (or 10 pm + 9 h). (d) The next day. (e) She lands at 7:00 am IST, so she should wait 30 minutes; London clocks will then show 2:00 am.
s: Part (a): 4:30 pm GMT
Part (b): 1:30 am GMT
Part (c): 7:00 am IST
Part (d): the next day
Part (e): wait 30 minutes; 2:00 am in London

questions.q: A ship sails due west from 45°E to 15°W, keeping its clocks on local time. By how much, and in which direction, must the clocks be changed over the whole voyage?
questions.a: The ship crosses 45 + 15 = 60 degrees of longitude, and 60 / 15 = 4 hours. Going west local time falls behind, so the clocks go back 4 hours. Forward is the eastward rule; 2 hours comes from 45 - 15 = 30 degrees, wrongly subtracting values on opposite sides of the Prime Meridian.

questions.q:
An imaginary country, Zarin, stretches from 60°E to 105°E. The Earth turns 15 degrees every hour.
(a) What is the difference in local time between Zarin's western and eastern edges?
(b) If every town kept its own local time, what would the local time be at the eastern edge when it is noon at the western edge?
(c) Zarin bases one standard time on the meridian exactly in its middle. Which meridian is that, and how far ahead of GMT is Zarin's standard time?
(d) At noon GMT, what do all clocks in Zarin show, and what is the local time then at the western edge and at the eastern edge?
(e) Zarin's law allows a single standard time only if no town's local time differs from the clocks by more than 2 hours. Using (d), find the largest gap anywhere in Zarin and say whether the law allows one standard time.
questions.a: (a) 105 - 60 = 45 degrees; 45 / 15 = 3 hours. (b) 3 hours later: 3 pm. (c) (60 + 105) / 2 = 82.5°E; 82.5 / 15 = 5.5 hours, so 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT. (d) The clocks show 5:30 pm. Local time at 60°E is 60 / 15 = 4 hours ahead of GMT, 4 pm; at 105°E it is 7 hours ahead, 7 pm. (e) The largest gap is 1 hour 30 minutes, at each edge (5:30 pm against 4 pm in the west and 7 pm in the east). That is within the 2-hour limit, so the law allows one standard time, which also avoids the inconvenience of many local times.
s: Part (a): 3 hours
Part (b): 3 pm
Part (c): 82.5°E, 5 h 30 min ahead of GMT
Part (d): clocks 5:30 pm; local 4 pm west, 7 pm east
Part (e): largest gap 1 h 30 min, within the 2-hour limit, so one standard time is allowed

questions.q:
An expedition's base camp is on the Prime Meridian. It must hold one radio call with three field stations at once, using local time at each place.
| Station | Longitude |
| P | 60°E |
| Q | 15°W |
| R | 105°E |
Every station can talk only between 8 am and 6 pm its own local time.
(a) When it is 12 noon at the base, what is the local time at P?
(b) At that moment, what is the local time at Q?
(c) Which station is 7 hours ahead of the base?
(d) The base can call at 12 noon or at 10 am base time. Which time works for all three stations? Show the check.
questions.a: (a) 60 / 15 = 4 hours ahead: 4 pm. (b) 15 / 15 = 1 hour behind: 11 am. (c) R: 105 / 15 = 7 hours ahead. (d) 10 am. At 12 noon, R would be at 7 pm, past 6 pm. At 10 am base time: P 2 pm, Q 9 am, R 5 pm, all within 8 am to 6 pm.
s: Part (a): 4 pm
Part (b): 11 am
Part (c): R
Part (d): 10 am, with every station checked

questions.q: Town A is at 29°N, 77°E and Town B at 13°N, 80°E. The Earth turns 15 degrees every hour. Town B's local time is ___ minutes ahead of Town A's.

The Earth turns 15 degrees every 60 minutes. A town's local time is 2 hours 20 minutes ahead of the local time at Greenwich.
(a) How many degrees from the Prime Meridian is the town, and on which side?
(b) What is the town's local time when it is 10:50 pm on Monday at Greenwich?
questions.a: (a) 60 / 15 = 4 minutes per degree; 2 h 20 min = 140 minutes; 140 / 4 = 35 degrees. It is ahead, so it lies east: 35°E. (b) 10:50 pm + 2 h 20 min = 1:10 am on Tuesday.
s: Part (a): 35°E, from 140 minutes at 4 minutes per degree
Part (b): 1:10 am on Tuesday

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. A difference of 45 degrees of longitude means a difference of 3 hours in local time.
2. Moving westward from the Prime Meridian, local time is ahead by one hour for every 15 degrees.
3. When it is noon at Greenwich, the local time at 30°E is 10 am, two hours behind.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only 1 is correct: 45 / 15 = 3 hours. 2 is false: going westward local time falls behind, not ahead. 3 is false: 30°E is east of the Prime Meridian, so it is two hours ahead, at 2 pm; 10 am is the time at 30°W.

questions.q: True or False? 'Indian Standard Time is based on one meridian, so the actual local time in most Indian towns is a little different from IST.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. A standard time is based on one meridian passing through the country; local time changes by one hour for every 15 degrees of longitude, so towns east or west of that meridian have local times ahead of or behind IST.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: standard time follows one meridian; local time varies with each town's longitude

questions.q:
Local time changes by one hour for every 15 degrees of longitude.
(a) When it is noon at Greenwich, what is the local time at 37.5°W?
(b) A radio show starts at 7:20 pm local time in a town at 52.5°E. What is the local time then at 37.5°W?
questions.a: (a) 37.5 / 15 = 2.5 hours, and going west the time is behind, so 12 noon - 2 h 30 min = 9:30 am. (b) The towns are 52.5 + 37.5 = 90 degrees apart, 90 / 15 = 6 hours, and 37.5°W is to the west, so 7:20 pm - 6 h = 1:20 pm.
s: Part (a): 9:30 am
Part (b): 1:20 pm, 6 hours behind

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When it is noon at Greenwich, the local time at 15°E is 1 pm.
Reason (R): The Earth turns 15 degrees every hour from west to east, so a place 15 degrees farther east is one hour ahead in local time.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: 15 degrees of eastward longitude equals one hour of the Earth's turn, so 15°E is one hour ahead of Greenwich.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Write a situation with two towns, their longitudes and a local time in one of them, whose answer is 'The local time in the second town is 4 hours behind the first.' Then show the working.
questions.a: Any consistent situation in which the second town lies 60 degrees west of the first, for example: Town P is at 75°E and Town Q at 15°E. It is 6 pm local time in P. Working: 75 - 15 = 60 degrees; 60 / 15 = 4 hours; Q is to the west, so it is behind: 2 pm.
s: Two towns whose longitudes differ by 60 degrees
The second town lies to the west of the first
Working: 60 / 15 = 4 hours behind

questions.q:
Read this message from a family group chat.
'Arjun's school concert in London will be shown live online from 4 pm to 6 pm London time; London keeps GMT. Arjun's own song is from 5:15 pm to 5:30 pm. The school will show a full repeat the next day from 10 am to 12 noon London time.'
Dadi in Kolkata goes to sleep at 11 pm, and every afternoon she is at the temple from 3 pm to 5 pm.
(a) At what time by IST does the live concert begin and end?
(b) At what times by IST is Arjun's song?
(c) At what times by IST does the repeat run?
(d) Dadi wants to see Arjun sing. Which showing should she watch, and until when? Justify using (a)-(c).
questions.a: (a) 4 pm + 5 h 30 min = 9:30 pm IST; 6 pm + 5 h 30 min = 11:30 pm IST. (b) 10:45 pm to 11:00 pm IST. (c) 3:30 pm to 5:30 pm IST. (d) The live show, from 9:30 pm until 11 pm. The live concert runs past her bedtime, but Arjun's song ends exactly at 11 pm, so she sees it and can then sleep. The repeat is at an easy hour, but the song comes 1 hour 15 minutes into it, at 4:45 pm to 5:00 pm IST, while she is at the temple.
s: Part (a): 9:30 pm to 11:30 pm IST
Part (b): 10:45 pm to 11:00 pm IST
