Part (c): 3:30 pm to 5:30 pm IST
Part (d): live until 11 pm; the song ends by bedtime, and the repeat clashes with the temple

questions.q: A country lies mostly in the 15-degree band centred on 30°E, but its eastern part reaches into the next band. On the time-zone map, the zone line bends round the whole country instead of following the meridian between the bands. Why?
questions.a: Countries adopt one standard time, and the zone lines respect each country's standard time, so they tend to follow international borders; the whole country stays on one time. Meridians do not bend; the bands are still the broad basis; Date Line bends are about dates, not this.
o: The line follows the border so the country keeps one standard time
The meridians themselves bend where they cross the country's land
Time zones no longer use the 15-degree bands as any guide at all
The line must bend away from the Date Line, which lies along its edge

questions.q:
A school in Pune is hosting an online quiz with two partner schools abroad. On the time-zone map, India's standard time is GMT +5:30, Country X's is GMT +9 and Country Y's is GMT -3. Each school can take part only between 8 am and 10 pm its own standard time. The first plan is to start at 7 pm IST.
(a) What is the time at Greenwich at 7 pm IST?
(b) What time is it then in Country X?
(c) What time is it then in Country Y?
(d) The organisers can start at 7 pm IST or at 5 pm IST. Which start time works for all three schools? Show the check.
questions.a: (a) 7 pm - 5 h 30 min = 1:30 pm GMT. (b) 1:30 pm + 9 h = 10:30 pm. (c) 1:30 pm - 3 h = 10:30 am. (d) 5 pm IST. At 7 pm IST Country X is at 10:30 pm, past its limit. At 5 pm IST it is 11:30 am GMT: India 5 pm, X 8:30 pm, Y 8:30 am, all within 8 am to 10 pm.
s: Part (a): 1:30 pm GMT
Part (b): 10:30 pm in Country X
Part (c): 10:30 am in Country Y
Part (d): 5 pm IST, with all three schools checked

questions.q: Arun flies from a country on GMT +12 to its neighbour on GMT -12, crossing the Date Line. He says, 'My watch will have to change by 24 hours, so the clock time will be completely different.' Show that the clock time need not change at all, but the date must.
questions.a: The two zones are 12 + 12 = 24 hours apart. 24 hours is exactly one full day, so the hour on the clock is the same in both, for example 9 am and 9 am. What differs is the date: the -12 side is one day behind, so 9 am Wednesday on the +12 side is 9 am Tuesday on the -12 side.
s: The zones differ by 12 + 12 = 24 hours
24 hours is one whole day, so the clock time is the same
Only the date changes, by one day

questions.q: True or False? 'Since time zones are 15 degrees wide, the lines between them on a world map are exactly the meridians at every 15 degrees.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Time zones broadly follow the 15-degree zones, but the lines dividing them are not fully straight: they respect each country's standard time and so tend to follow international borders.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the lines bend to follow international borders and each country's standard time

questions.q:
An imaginary country, Veda, stretches from 22.5°E to 52.5°E. Its eastern border with its neighbour zigzags and is not a meridian. Local time changes by one hour every 15 degrees.
(a) If time zones were exact 15-degree bands, each centred on a meridian at 0°, 15°E, 30°E and so on, which bands would Veda cover, and what would their times be with respect to GMT?
(b) Veda adopts one standard time based on the meridian in its middle. Which meridian is that, and what is Veda's standard time with respect to GMT?
(c) Using (a) and (b), explain why Veda's time is not a whole number of hours from GMT.
(d) Explain why, on a world time-zone map, the line between Veda's zone and its neighbour's will follow the zigzag border rather than a meridian.
(e) Judge the statement 'Time zones are based on longitude, but their final shape is decided by countries.' The statement holds only if (a)-(d) give evidence for both halves; say which parts give which.
questions.a: (a) Two bands: the one centred on 30°E (22.5°E to 37.5°E), GMT +2, and the one centred on 45°E (37.5°E to 52.5°E), GMT +3. (b) (22.5 + 52.5) / 2 = 37.5°E; 37.5 / 15 = 2.5, so GMT +2 hours 30 minutes. (c) Veda chose a meridian of its own, which falls on the edge between the two bands, not on a band's centre, so its time falls between +2 and +3. (d) Zone lines respect each country's standard time and so tend to follow international borders; following a meridian would split Veda between two times. (e) The statement holds. (a) shows the longitude basis: 15 degrees for each hour. (b), (c) and (d) show the countries' part: Veda chose its own meridian and half-hour time, and its border, not a meridian, fixes where its zone ends.
s: Part (a): two bands, GMT +2 and GMT +3
Part (b): 37.5°E, GMT +2 h 30 min
Part (c): the chosen meridian lies between band centres, so the time falls between +2 and +3
Part (d): zone lines follow borders to keep one standard time
Part (e): holds; (a) gives the longitude basis, (b)-(d) the countries' choices

questions.q: A cruise ship's newsletter at breakfast was dated Thursday. That same afternoon, with no night having passed, the captain announced that the date was now Friday. What most likely happened?
questions.a: Crossing the International Date Line westward adds a day, so Thursday became Friday during the afternoon. Going east would subtract a day (back to Wednesday); crossing the Prime Meridian changes no date; entering a +12 zone without crossing the line changes no date.
o: It crossed the Date Line sailing west
It crossed the Date Line sailing east
It crossed the Prime Meridian going west
It sailed into a country on GMT +12

questions.q:
India's longitudes extend from about 68°E to 97°E, yet the whole country uses one Indian Standard Time.
(a) How many degrees of longitude does India span?
(b) Using 4 minutes per degree, what is the difference in local time between India's western and eastern limits?
(c) Why does India still keep one standard time instead of using local times?
questions.a: (a) 97 - 68 = 29 degrees. (b) 29 x 4 = 116 minutes = 1 hour 56 minutes. (c) It would not be convenient for a country to use many local times, so India, like most countries, adopts one standard time based on a meridian passing through it.
s: Part (a): 29 degrees
Part (b): 1 hour 56 minutes
Part (c): many local times would be inconvenient, so one standard time is used

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. The International Date Line lies roughly opposite the Prime Meridian.
2. A traveller crossing the Date Line westward adds a day.
3. The Date Line runs exactly along the 180° meridian everywhere.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 are correct: the line is at approximately 180°, opposite the Prime Meridian, and crossing it westward adds a day. 3 is false: the line deviates in places to avoid dividing some countries into two different days.

questions.q:
A ship sails out of the +12 time zone and straight into the -12 time zone, crossing the International Date Line.
(a) In which direction is it sailing? Explain.
(b) Using (a), what must the crew do to the date?
questions.a: (a) Eastward. Moving east from Greenwich the zones add hours, so the +12 zone lies on the eastern-longitude side of the line and the -12 zone on the western-longitude side; going from +12 to -12 means crossing from 180°E to 180°W, moving east. (b) Subtract a day, as when crossing eastward (for example, Monday to Sunday).
s: Part (a): eastward, from the 180°E side to the 180°W side
Part (b): subtract a day

questions.q: A plane leaves a city on GMT +3 at 10 pm on Monday, local time, and flies for 4 hours to a city on GMT +8. What is the local time when it lands?
questions.a: 7 am on Tuesday. 10 pm Monday at +3 is 7 pm Monday GMT; 4 hours later it is 11 pm Monday GMT; +8 makes it 7 am Tuesday. 2 am adds only the flight time; 11 pm Monday is the GMT time; 9 pm Monday subtracts the 5-hour zone gap instead of adding it.

questions.q:
Suppose time zones were exact 15-degree bands, each centred on a meridian at 0°, 15°E, 30°E and so on (so the band centred on 75°E runs from 67.5°E to 82.5°E).
(a) India's longitudes extend from about 68°E to 97°E. Which bands would India cover, and what times with respect to GMT would they give?
(b) India actually uses one standard time, GMT +5:30. Using (a), what does this show about how real time zones are fixed?
questions.a: (a) Two bands: the one centred on 75°E (67.5°E to 82.5°E), GMT +5, and the one centred on 90°E (82.5°E to 97.5°E), GMT +6. (b) Real zones only broadly follow the bands. India adopted one standard time for the whole country, 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT, between the +5 and +6 of the two bands, because each country chooses its own standard time based on a meridian passing through it.
s: Part (a): two bands, GMT +5 and GMT +6
Part (b): one chosen standard time between them; zones only broadly follow the bands

questions.q: On the time-zone map a country is marked -4. When it is 3 pm at Greenwich, the clocks in that country show ___ am.

A company in a country on GMT +12 holds a weekly video meeting with a partner office in a country on GMT -11, across the International Date Line. Both offices work from 9 am to 5 pm, Monday to Friday, by their own clocks.
(a) How many hours apart are the clocks of the two offices?
(b) When it is 9 am on Tuesday in the +12 office, what time and day is it in the -11 office?
(c) Why would 9 am on Monday in the +12 office be a poor choice?
(d) The partner suggests 3 pm on Friday by its own clock; the company suggests 9 am on Tuesday by its own clock. Which suggestion works for both offices? Show the check.
questions.a: (a) 12 + 11 = 23 hours. (b) 23 hours earlier: 10 am on Monday. (c) It would be 10 am on Sunday in the -11 office, a day it does not work. (d) The company's: 9 am Tuesday (+12) is 10 am Monday (-11), inside both offices' hours. The partner's 3 pm Friday (-11) is 2 pm Saturday in the +12 office, when it is closed.
s: Part (a): 23 hours
Part (b): 10 am on Monday
Part (c): it is Sunday in the -11 office
Part (d): the company's time; the partner's falls on Saturday at +12

questions.q:
A sailor leaves Chennai and sails eastward all the way round the world, back to Chennai. Every time she enters a new 15-degree band she sets her watch to that band's local time.
(a) Does she move her watch forward or back each time? Why?
(b) How many such changes does she make in a full circle of 360 degrees?
(c) By how much in total has she moved her watch, and what is that equal to?
(d) What must she do when she crosses the International Date Line eastward?
(e) Explain how (c) and (d) together keep her calendar correct when she reaches home.
questions.a: (a) Forward: going east, local time is ahead by one hour for every 15 degrees. (b) 360 / 15 = 24 changes. (c) 24 x 1 hour = 24 hours forward, a whole day. (d) Subtract a day. (e) The 24 hours gained by moving the watch forward add up to one extra day; subtracting one day at the Date Line cancels it, so her date agrees with the date at home.
s: Part (a): forward, since east is ahead
Part (b): 24 changes
Part (c): 24 hours, one whole day
Part (d): subtract a day at the Date Line
Part (e): the day gained is cancelled by the day subtracted

questions.q: Kavya says: 'The International Date Line has to bend away from the 180° meridian in places; if it did not, some countries would have two different dates at the same moment.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. Crossing the Date Line changes the date by one day, because the +12 and -12 zones touch there. If the line cut straight through a country, the parts on either side would be on different days at the same moment. So the line is only approximately at 180°: it deviates in places to avoid dividing some countries into two different days.
s: Verdict: yes
Crossing the line changes the date by a day
The line deviates to keep each country on one day

questions.q:
Moving east from Greenwich the time zones are numbered +1, +2, +3 ... and moving west -1, -2, -3 ..., each zone broadly 15 degrees wide.
(a) Near which longitude do the +12 and -12 zones meet? Show the working.
(b) Why must the date change where they meet, when crossing between two neighbouring zones near Greenwich changes only the hour?
questions.a: (a) 12 x 15 = 180 degrees east and 180 degrees west, so they meet near 180° longitude, opposite the Prime Meridian. (b) The +12 and -12 zones are 12 + 12 = 24 hours apart, a whole day, so the two sides show the same hour on different dates. Neighbouring zones near Greenwich differ by only one hour.
s: Part (a): 12 x 15 = 180, so near 180°
Part (b): +12 and -12 are 24 hours (a day) apart; neighbours differ by one hour

questions.q:
Match each journey in Column A with what happens in Column B.
Column A: 1. crossing the International Date Line eastward  2. crossing the International Date Line westward  3. crossing the Prime Meridian eastward  4. moving east from a -3 zone into a -2 zone
Column B: a. the date goes back one day  b. the date goes forward one day  c. the hemisphere changes but the date does not  d. clocks go forward one hour
questions.a: Eastward across the Date Line a day is subtracted; westward a day is added. Crossing the Prime Meridian takes you from the Western into the Eastern Hemisphere but changes no date. From -3 to -2 the zone is one hour nearer GMT going east, so clocks go forward one hour.

questions.q: On the time-zone map a country is marked -5. When the clocks there show 8 pm, what time is it at Greenwich?
questions.a: A -5 country is 5 hours behind GMT, so Greenwich is 5 hours ahead of it: 8 pm + 5 hours = 1 am the next day. 3 pm subtracts instead of adding; 1 pm and 3 am use wrong hour counts.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Every country in the world has exactly one standard time.
Reason (R): Russia has 11 time zones.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false and R is true. Some countries, like Russia, Canada and the USA, are too large for a single time zone; Russia's 11 zones are an example that disproves A.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
The USA has six time zones side by side and Russia has eleven. Take neighbouring zones to differ by one hour.
(a) How many times must a traveller going from the westernmost to the easternmost of the USA's six zones reset her watch, and in which direction each time?
(b) Another traveller crosses all of Russia's zones from east to west, and later all of the USA's zones from west to east. In all, how many times does he reset his watch, and by how many hours, forward or back, has his watch been moved overall?
questions.a: (a) Five times, forward: six zones side by side have five boundaries between them, and going east the time is ahead. (b) Russia: 11 zones have 10 boundaries, each crossed going west, so 10 resets back; USA: 5 resets forward. In all 10 + 5 = 15 resets, and overall 10 - 5 = 5 hours back.
s: Part (a): 5 resets, forward each time
Part (b): 15 resets, net 5 hours back

questions.q:
An island country has some islands at 178°E and others at 172°W.
(a) If the International Date Line ran exactly along 180°, what would be true about the dates on the two groups of islands at the same moment?
(b) What does the real Date Line do in such places, and why?
questions.a: (a) The 180° line would pass between them, so the two groups would be on different dates at the same moment, one day apart. (b) The real line deviates from 180° in places, going round such a country so that the whole country keeps one date.
s: Part (a): the line would split them onto dates a day apart
Part (b): the line bends round the country to keep it on one date
